• By recommending a phased reduction in these mandatory reserve requirements, the committee aimed to enhance the availability of credit for productive commercial lending, improve banks' profitability and operational flexibility, and move the banking system away from excessive, centrally directed control toward a more market-oriented, efficient financial sector.

• The committee's recommendations also covered other significant areas, including prudential norms for asset classification and provisioning (addressing Non-Performing Assets/NPAs), capital adequacy requirements aligned with international (Basel) standards, and greater operational autonomy for banks — collectively reshaping the foundation of India's modern banking regulatory framework.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• A second Narasimham Committee report (1998) further built on these reforms, recommending additional measures including bank mergers/consolidation, stronger capital adequacy norms, and enhanced governance and risk-management standards for Indian banks.

• The reduction in CRR/SLR requirements over subsequent years (from very high pre-1991 levels to progressively lower levels) significantly increased the loanable funds available to India's banking sector, supporting the broader economic growth agenda of the liberalisation era.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1: Incorrect — the Narasimham Committee's reforms moved in the opposite direction, recommending reduced, not expanded, directed credit programmes and greater interest rate flexibility (moving toward deregulation), not "tighter interest rate controls".

• Option 2: Incorrect — the committee's reforms were part of a broader liberalisation agenda promoting greater private participation and competition in banking, not "nationalisation of private banks to ensure state dominance," which would represent the opposite, more state-controlled approach.

• Option 4: Incorrect — the committee did not recommend "complete privatisation of all public sector banks"; while it did support greater competition, operational autonomy, and some reduction of government's role in day-to-day bank management, wholesale complete privatisation of all PSU banks was not among its core recommendations.

question: What does the term 'Hindu Rate of Growth' signify in the context of India's economic history, and what were the structural factors that contributed to this phenomenon during the pre-liberalization period (1950s-1980s)?
option_1: A growth model based on Hindu philosophical principles of minimalism and austerity
option_2: A period of high economic growth during the license-permit era, driven by state-led industrialization
option_3: A prolonged phase of low and stagnant economic growth averaging around 3-3.5% annually, caused by excessive state control, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and limited private sector participation under a socialist policy framework
option_4: A rapid increase in GDP driven by population growth among Hindu-majority states
solution_text:
The correct answer is A prolonged phase of low and stagnant economic growth averaging around 3-3.5% annually, caused by excessive state control, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and limited private sector participation under a socialist policy framework.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The term "Hindu Rate of Growth" was coined by Indian economist Raj Krishna to describe India's persistently low and stagnant economic growth rate — averaging roughly 3-3.5% per annum — that characterised the Indian economy from the 1950s through the 1980s, a period marked by extensive state control over economic activity.

• The term specifically referred to structural, policy-driven factors — including the restrictive "License-Permit-Quota Raj" industrial licensing regime, heavy state ownership and control over key industries, bureaucratic inefficiencies, limited scope for private sector initiative, and inward-looking trade protectionism — rather than any genuine connection to Hindu religion or philosophy; the term used "Hindu" somewhat ironically/critically to characterise the fatalistic, seemingly unavoidable low-growth trajectory the economy appeared locked into under this policy framework.

• This period of sluggish growth stood in notable contrast to the significantly higher growth rates achieved by many East Asian economies during the same decades, and it was precisely this prolonged growth stagnation, compounded by the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, that catalysed India's decisive shift toward economic liberalisation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raj Krishna coined this term in the 1970s, and it became a widely used shorthand in Indian economic discourse for critiquing the perceived inefficiencies of the pre-1991 socialist-inspired, state-controlled economic model.

• Following the 1991 reforms, India's growth rate accelerated substantially over subsequent decades, eventually reaching an average of 6-8% or higher in various periods, marking a clear structural break from the earlier "Hindu Rate of Growth" era.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1: Incorrect — the term has no actual connection to Hindu religious or philosophical principles of minimalism/austerity; it was a critical, somewhat ironic economic label describing structural policy failures, not a genuine religiously-inspired economic model.

• Option 2: Incorrect — this describes the opposite scenario; the "Hindu Rate of Growth" specifically refers to a period of low, stagnant growth (roughly 3-3.5%), not "high economic growth," during the license-permit era.

• Option 4: Incorrect — the term is unrelated to "population growth among Hindu-majority states" driving GDP; it is a macroeconomic term describing India's overall national growth trajectory shaped by structural economic policy factors, not a demographic or religiously-differentiated regional phenomenon.

question: Which Five Year Plan period is associated with the first implementation of the Green Revolution?
option_1: Second Plan
option_2: Third Plan
option_3: Fourth Plan
solution_text:
The correct answer is Third Plan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Green Revolution in India — the introduction of High-Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, expanded irrigation, chemical fertilisers, and modern agricultural techniques, particularly for wheat and rice — is generally associated with the mid-1960s, a period that falls within the timeframe of the Third Five-Year Plan (1961-1966), making this the standard reference point in most competitive exam contexts for the Green Revolution's initial implementation.

• The Green Revolution's early, most visible successes were concentrated in states like Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh, regions with favourable irrigation infrastructure and agro-climatic conditions suited to the new HYV seed varieties (especially wheat).

• The initiative is closely linked to the pioneering agricultural scientist Dr. M.S. Swaminathan, often called the "Father of the Green Revolution in India," who played a central role in adapting and promoting high-yielding wheat varieties (building on research by Nobel laureate Norman Borlaug) suited to Indian growing conditions.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Green Revolution significantly boosted India's foodgrain self-sufficiency, helping the country move away from a period of substantial food-grain imports and periodic food shortages toward eventual self-sufficiency in staple cereal production by the 1970s.

• While transformative for cereal production, the Green Revolution has also been critiqued for its regionally uneven impact (concentrated mainly in a few well-irrigated states) and its environmental consequences (including groundwater depletion and soil health concerns from intensive fertiliser/pesticide use), issues that continue to shape Indian agricultural policy discussions today.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Second Plan): The Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61), based on the Mahalanobis model, focused primarily on rapid heavy industrialisation, predating the Green Revolution's actual implementation, which began somewhat later.

• Option 3 (Fourth Plan): The Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-74) came after the Green Revolution's initial rollout (which began around 1966); by this period, the Green Revolution was already underway and expanding, rather than being newly "first implemented".

• Option 4 (Fifth Plan): The Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974-79) is associated with other priorities, including the "Garibi Hatao" (Remove Poverty) programme, and came well after the Green Revolution's initial implementation phase in the mid-1960s.

question: In India, the revenue collected from agricultural income tax is allocated to which level of government?
option_1: State Governments
option_2: Central Government
option_3: Collected by State Governments, delivered to Central Government
option_4: Collected by Central Government, delivered to State Governments
solution_text:
The correct answer is State Governments.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under India's constitutional distribution of taxation powers (Seventh Schedule), "Taxes on agricultural income" falls under Entry 46 of the State List, meaning State Legislatures have exclusive authority to levy and collect tax on agricultural income, and the resulting revenue belongs entirely to the respective State Governments, not the Union/Central Government.

• This is a deliberate constitutional distinction from "income tax" in general (covering non-agricultural income), which falls under Entry 82 of the Union List, making it a Central Government tax — highlighting the specific carve-out for agricultural income taxation as a State subject, reflecting agriculture's status as primarily a state-governed sector in India's federal structure.

• In practice, however, most Indian states have historically chosen not to actively levy or effectively collect agricultural income tax (for various political, administrative, and socio-economic reasons), even though they constitutionally possess this taxation power — a subject of ongoing policy debate regarding India's overall tax base and agricultural taxation policy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The distinction between agricultural income (State List, Entry 46) and non-agricultural income tax (Union List, Entry 82) is a frequently tested constitutional/taxation distinction in Indian competitive examinations, given its relevance to India's federal fiscal architecture.

• Some states, such as Kerala, Assam, and West Bengal, have at various points in history actually levied and collected agricultural income tax (particularly on plantation crops like tea, rubber and coffee), illustrating the practical, if limited, exercise of this state-level taxation power.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (Central Government): Incorrect — agricultural income tax is specifically a State List subject (Entry 46), not part of the Union Government's general income tax authority (which covers non-agricultural income under Union List Entry 82).

• Option 3 (Collected by State, delivered to Central): Incorrect — agricultural income tax revenue, when collected, is retained by and belongs to the State Government itself; it is not collected by states merely to be transferred/delivered to the Central Government.

• Option 4 (Collected by Central, delivered to State): Incorrect — the Central Government does not collect agricultural income tax at all, since this is exclusively a state taxation subject under the Constitution, not a Union-collected, state-shared tax.

question: Why is the Indian Ocean Region critical in global geopolitics?
option_1: It is the birthplace of democracy
option_2: Over 80% of global oil trade passes through its sea lanes
option_3: It is the least militarized zone
solution_text:
The correct answer is Over 80% of global oil trade passes through its sea lanes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian Ocean Region (IOR) holds immense strategic and economic significance in global geopolitics primarily because a very large share — commonly cited as over 80% — of the world's maritime oil trade transits through its critical sea lanes of communication (SLOCs), passing through key chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz, Strait of Malacca, and Bab-el-Mandeb.

• This makes the Indian Ocean a vital artery for global energy security and international trade, linking major oil-producing regions in the Middle East with key consuming markets in Asia (including India, China, Japan, and South Korea) and beyond, explaining why numerous major powers (India, the US, China, and others) maintain significant strategic and naval interests in the region.

• India's own maritime strategy, articulated through initiatives like SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region), reflects this recognition of the Indian Ocean's critical importance for both national security and economic prosperity, given India's central geographic position astride these vital sea lanes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key chokepoints within or adjacent to the Indian Ocean Region — narrow maritime passages through which shipping traffic is concentrated — are considered particularly strategically sensitive, as any disruption (due to conflict, piracy, or blockade) at these points could significantly impact global energy supplies and trade flows.

• The growing strategic competition in the Indian Ocean Region, sometimes discussed in the context of the broader "Indo-Pacific" framework, involves multiple major powers seeking to secure naval access, basing arrangements, and influence across this economically and strategically vital maritime space.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1: Incorrect — the Indian Ocean Region is not historically characterised or recognised as "the birthplace of democracy" (a description more commonly, if loosely, associated with ancient Athens/Greece); this is not the reason for its contemporary geopolitical significance.

• Option 3: Incorrect — the Indian Ocean Region is, in fact, a highly militarised and strategically contested zone, with numerous naval deployments and strategic interests from multiple major powers, not "the least militarized zone".

• Option 4: Incorrect — the Indian Ocean is not "entirely under UN control"; it comprises international waters alongside numerous sovereign nations' territorial waters and Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs), with no single UN governing authority controlling the entire region.

question: The establishment of the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) during the 2023 G20 Summit has been viewed as a significant move in shaping international trade routes. Which of the following options best reflects India's strategic advantage in IMEC when compared to China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)?
option_1: IMEC bypasses the Suez Canal and is backed by Russia
option_2: IMEC connects India to Russia directly via Arctic shipping lanes
option_3: IMEC enables India to access Europe through a US-backed, secure, and rules-based infrastructure
option_4: IMEC involves military deployment across the Arabian Peninsula
solution_text:
The correct answer is IMEC enables India to access Europe through a US-backed, secure, and rules-based infrastructure.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), announced during the 2023 G20 Summit in New Delhi, is a proposed multi-modal transport and economic connectivity corridor linking India, the Middle East (UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Israel), and Europe, involving a combination of rail and shipping links, and is backed by a coalition including India, the United States, the European Union, and several Gulf/Middle Eastern nations.

• A key strategic advantage frequently highlighted for IMEC, in contrast to China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), is that it is positioned as a transparent, rules-based, and financially sustainable infrastructure framework, backed by democratic partners including the US and EU — addressing concerns often raised about BRI projects, such as issues of debt sustainability, lack of transparency, and strategic dependency for participating countries.

• For India specifically, IMEC offers a strategically valuable alternative connectivity route to Europe that bypasses Pakistan entirely (unlike potential overland routes through South Asia) and reduces dependence on routes/infrastructure associated with China's BRI, aligning with India's broader interest in diversifying and securing its international trade and connectivity options.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• IMEC is seen as complementing existing India-led connectivity initiatives such as the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) (connecting India to Russia/Central Asia via Iran) and the Chabahar Port project, together reflecting India's broader multi-pronged approach to enhancing international trade connectivity while reducing single-corridor dependency.

• The corridor's proposed structure includes an Eastern Corridor (connecting India to the Arabian Gulf) and a Northern Corridor (connecting the Arabian Gulf to Europe), envisioning integrated rail, shipping, and even digital/energy connectivity infrastructure.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1: Incorrect — IMEC is not "backed by Russia"; it is backed by a coalition including India, the US, EU and Gulf nations, and while it does offer an alternative route avoiding certain traditional chokepoints, describing it as "Russia-backed" misrepresents its actual sponsoring coalition.

• Option 2: Incorrect — IMEC does not involve "Arctic shipping lanes" connecting India directly to Russia; this description is unrelated to IMEC's actual proposed India-Middle East-Europe route structure.

• Option 4: Incorrect — IMEC is fundamentally an economic and infrastructure connectivity initiative (rail, shipping, trade), not a "military deployment" framework; describing it in militarised terms misrepresents its stated civilian/economic purpose and framing.

question: Why was the 2011 National Games in Jharkhand regarded as a technological milestone in the history of the event?

option_2: Live hologram commentary in stadiums
option_3: Use of AI bots for scoring evaluation

• The 34th National Games, held in Jharkhand (Ranchi) in 2011, is noted in Indian sporting history as an event that introduced notable technological/administrative innovations for the National Games format, with the adoption of e-ticketing systems and online athlete registration representing a significant modernisation step compared to earlier, more paper-based/manual editions of the Games.

• This move toward digitised event management — covering ticketing and athlete registration processes — reflected a broader shift in Indian sports administration toward more efficient, technology-enabled organisational practices, setting something of a precedent for subsequent editions of the National Games and other major domestic sporting events.

• The 2011 National Games in Jharkhand also featured the mascot "Chhawa" (a baby deer) and were held primarily in Ranchi, with the event drawing participation from various Indian states and Union Territories across a range of sporting disciplines.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The National Games of India, the country's flagship multi-sport event akin to a domestic "mini-Olympics," rotates its host state/city periodically and has, over successive editions, progressively incorporated modernised organisational and technological practices in venue management, ticketing, and athlete administration.

• Jharkhand's hosting of the 2011 National Games also spurred the development of significant sporting infrastructure in Ranchi, including venues that continue to support the state's sporting activities today.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (Live hologram commentary in stadiums): Hologram-based commentary technology is a considerably more advanced/futuristic concept not associated with the 2011 National Games' actual technological milestones, which centred on more foundational digitisation (ticketing/registration), not hologram displays.

question: The role of the goalkeeper in modern hockey has evolved dramatically due to:
option_1: Change in jersey color rules
option_2: Use of heavier sticks
option_3: Introduction of advanced protective gear and aerial attacks
solution_text:
The correct answer is Introduction of advanced protective gear and aerial attacks.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The role of the goalkeeper in modern field hockey has transformed substantially over recent decades, largely driven by the introduction of significantly advanced protective equipment — including improved helmets, padded body armour, leg guards, and kickers — which has allowed goalkeepers to adopt far more aggressive, dynamic defensive techniques, including diving, blocking with multiple body parts, and confidently facing high-speed shots without the injury risks that limited earlier generations of goalkeepers.

• Simultaneously, the growing prevalence and tactical sophistication of aerial attacks/passes in modern hockey (lofted balls played over defenders to switch play or create scoring opportunities) has required goalkeepers to develop enhanced positional awareness, reflexes, and shot-stopping techniques specifically suited to reading and reacting to these elevated, fast-moving aerial deliveries.

• Together, these developments — improved protective technology enabling bolder technique, combined with evolving attacking tactics requiring greater goalkeeping skill and anticipation — have fundamentally reshaped what is expected of a modern hockey goalkeeper compared to earlier eras of the sport.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Modern field hockey has also seen substantial rule and playing-surface changes over time — including the shift to synthetic/artificial turf (significantly increasing game speed) and periodic adjustments to gameplay rules (such as the introduction of the "self-pass" and structuring matches into four quarters instead of two halves) — all contributing to the sport's overall increased pace and tactical evolution, which in turn has shaped the demands placed on goalkeepers.

• India has a rich historical legacy in field hockey, having won multiple Olympic gold medals, particularly during the sport's earlier decades, and the men's team's bronze medal finish at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics (2021) marked a notable modern-era Olympic hockey achievement, ending a long medal drought.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Change in jersey color rules): Jersey colour regulations are a minor administrative/uniform-related matter and have no substantive connection to the evolving tactical or technical role of the goalkeeper in modern hockey.

• Option 2 (Use of heavier sticks): Modern hockey has generally trended toward lighter, more technologically advanced composite sticks for field players (for greater control and speed), not "heavier sticks," and this is unrelated to the specific evolution of the goalkeeper's role.

• Option 4 (Removal of offside rule): While the offside rule was indeed removed from field hockey in 1998, this rule change primarily affected overall attacking play and team tactical structure broadly, rather than being the specific, defining driver of the goalkeeper's evolved technical/defensive role, which is more directly attributable to protective gear advancements and aerial-attack tactics.

question: What is the significance of the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup in Indian hockey history?
option_1: It's India's first hosted World Cup
option_2: It's the only event India has never won
option_3: It serves as a prestigious international annual invitational tournament

• The Sultan Azlan Shah Cup is typically held in Ipoh, Malaysia, and has featured strong historical participation from leading hockey nations including India, Pakistan, Australia, South Korea, Germany, and New Zealand, among others, cementing its reputation as a significant annual fixture on the international hockey calendar.

• Malaysia's strong hockey tradition and consistent hosting of this tournament reflect the sport's considerable popularity and institutional support within the country, alongside its own competitive national hockey programme.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (India's first hosted World Cup): Incorrect — the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup is not a World Cup and is not hosted by India; it is an invitational tournament hosted annually in Malaysia, distinct from any FIH-sanctioned World Cup event.

• Option 2 (Only event India has never won): Incorrect — India has, in fact, won the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup multiple times over the tournament's history, directly contradicting the claim that it is an event India has "never won".

question: Which Indian athlete faced suspension in 2021 for testing positive for banned substances despite securing Olympic qualification?

option_3: Manjeet Singh

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA), operating in alignment with the global World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) framework, has intensified anti-doping testing and enforcement in recent years, part of a broader effort to improve the integrity and international credibility of Indian athletics.

question: The Indian Desert lies to the northwest of the Aravalli Hills and is characterized by arid conditions and shifting sand dunes. Which of the following is the correct reason for the formation of the Indian Desert?
option_1: It lies in the tropical rainforest region
option_2: It is located in the windward side of the Western Ghats
option_3: It lies in the rain shadow region of the Aravalli Hills
option_4: It receives heavy rainfall from the northeast monsoon
solution_text:
The correct answer is It lies in the rain shadow region of the Aravalli Hills.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Indian Desert (Thar Desert), located in Rajasthan to the northwest of the Aravalli Range, owes its arid, low-rainfall conditions substantially to its position relative to the Aravallis, which — running largely parallel to the direction of the monsoon winds rather than perpendicular/obstructing them — fail to effectively intercept and cause the monsoon-bearing winds to release significant rainfall over the desert region, leaving it in what is often described as a broad rain-shadow-like arid zone.

• This orientation of the Aravalli Hills (running roughly southwest to northeast, largely parallel to the southwest monsoon winds arriving from the Arabian Sea) means the winds pass over the region largely without being forced upward and cooled sufficiently to release substantial precipitation, contributing significantly to the desert's persistently dry conditions, in combination with other factors like the region's distance from moisture sources and local atmospheric subsidence patterns.

• The Thar Desert's aridity is further reinforced by very low and highly erratic annual rainfall (often below 250mm in its most arid western parts), extreme temperature variations, and strong winds that contribute to the characteristic shifting sand dunes for which the region is well known.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Thar Desert spans a substantial area across Rajasthan (with smaller extensions into Gujarat, Punjab, Haryana, and across the border into Pakistan's Sindh region), making it one of the world's most densely populated desert regions despite its harsh climatic conditions.

• India's major desert-reclamation and development initiatives — such as the Indira Gandhi Canal — have historically aimed to bring irrigation to parts of this arid region, supporting agriculture and settlement in otherwise water-scarce desert areas.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Tropical rainforest region): Incorrect — the Indian Desert is characterised by extreme aridity, the complete opposite of a "tropical rainforest region," which would instead feature abundant rainfall and dense vegetation.

• Option 2 (Windward side of Western Ghats): Incorrect — the Indian/Thar Desert is located in Rajasthan, geographically distant from and unrelated to the Western Ghats (a separate mountain range along India's western coast); the windward side of the Western Ghats is, in fact, one of India's highest-rainfall regions, not a desert.

• Option 4 (Heavy rainfall from northeast monsoon): Incorrect — the Indian Desert receives very low, not heavy, rainfall, and India's northeast monsoon (a winter monsoon phenomenon) primarily affects the southeastern coast (Tamil Nadu), not the northwestern desert region of Rajasthan.

question: India's vast coastline stretches for over 7,500 kilometers, significantly impacting its climate, economy, and coastal lifestyles. Which among the following coastal plains is known for its lagoons, backwaters, and comparatively recent geological formation?
option_1: Konkan Coast
option_2: Coromandel Coast
option_3: Malabar Coast
solution_text:
The correct answer is Malabar Coast.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Malabar Coast, forming the southern portion of India's western coastal plain (running along Kerala and parts of southern Karnataka), is particularly renowned for its extensive network of lagoons and backwaters — most famously exemplified by Vembanad Lake, Kerala's largest lagoon/backwater system — which have made this region a globally recognised destination for houseboat tourism and distinctive coastal ecology.

• Geologically, the Malabar Coast is considered a relatively young/recently formed coastal region, shaped significantly by ongoing processes of sediment deposition, wave action, and the dynamic interaction between the Arabian Sea and numerous west-flowing rivers, contributing to its distinctive network of interconnected lagoons, canals, and backwater channels.

• This makes the Malabar Coast geologically and geomorphologically distinct from India's other major coastal plain regions, which are generally characterised by different combinations of features (such as deltaic formations, older/harder rock coastlines, or different sedimentary histories).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's western coastal plain is broadly divided into the Konkan Coast (from Maharashtra/Goa southward) and the Malabar Coast (further south, through Kerala), while the eastern coastal plain comprises the Northern Circars (Odisha/northern Andhra Pradesh) and the Coromandel Coast (further south, through Tamil Nadu), each with distinct geomorphological characteristics.

• Kerala's backwater network, centred around systems like Vembanad Lake, supports a unique regional economy and culture, including traditional houseboat (kettuvallam) tourism, fishing, and coconut-based coastal agriculture, alongside significant biodiversity value.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Konkan Coast): The Konkan Coast, spanning Maharashtra and Goa, is characterised more by its rocky, indented coastline with numerous estuaries, but it is not specifically renowned for the same extensive lagoon/backwater network that distinctively characterises the Malabar Coast further south.

• Option 2 (Coromandel Coast): Located along Tamil Nadu on India's eastern coast, the Coromandel Coast is instead characterised by its broader, flatter plains and significant river deltas (such as the Kaveri delta), not the lagoon/backwater system that defines the Malabar Coast.

question: The photoelectric effect demonstrated that:
option_1: Light behaves only as a wave.
option_2: Electrons can be created by heating metal.
option_3: Light energy is quantized and delivered in discrete packets, confirming the particle nature of light.
option_4: Energy conservation does not apply to photons.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Light energy is quantized and delivered in discrete packets, confirming the particle nature of light.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The photoelectric effect — the emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency shines upon it — was famously explained by Albert Einstein in 1905 (earning him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921), who proposed that light energy is quantised, delivered in discrete packets called "photons," rather than as a continuous wave, as classical wave theory of light had previously assumed.

• Einstein's explanation showed that each photon carries a specific amount of energy proportional to its frequency (E = hf, where h is Planck's constant), and that electron emission depends on whether individual photons carry enough energy to overcome the metal's "work function" (the minimum energy needed to eject an electron) — critically, increasing light intensity alone (more photons) does not cause emission if each individual photon's energy/frequency is too low, a finding inexplicable under purely classical wave theory.

• This breakthrough explanation provided crucial early evidence for the particle-like (quantum) nature of light, becoming a foundational pillar of modern quantum mechanics and demonstrating light's fundamental wave-particle duality (behaving as both wave and particle depending on the context/experiment).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The photoelectric effect's threshold-frequency behaviour (where light below a certain frequency, however intense, produces no electron emission) was a key experimental puzzle that classical wave theory could not adequately explain, making Einstein's quantised-photon explanation a landmark achievement in early 20th-century physics.

• The photoelectric effect has significant practical applications, including in solar cells (photovoltaic technology), photodiodes, and various light-sensing/photodetector devices widely used in modern electronics and renewable energy technology.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1: Incorrect — the photoelectric effect specifically demonstrated the opposite: that light cannot be explained by wave theory alone, and must also be understood as behaving like discrete particles (photons) under certain conditions, establishing light's dual wave-particle nature rather than confirming it behaves "only as a wave".

• Option 2: Incorrect — the photoelectric effect involves the emission of pre-existing electrons already present within the metal (ejected when they absorb sufficient photon energy), not the "creation" of new electrons through heating; this option misrepresents the actual underlying physical process.

• Option 4: Incorrect — the photoelectric effect is entirely consistent with, and indeed relies upon, the conservation of energy principle (photon energy is transferred to the electron, partly overcoming the work function and partly becoming the electron's kinetic energy); energy conservation very much does apply to photons in this and all other physical processes.

question: Which of the given statements correctly describes the term Jagati in a Nagara-style temple?
option_1: Jagati is the spire that houses the deity inside.
option_2: Jagati is the topmost element of the temple's shikhara.
option_3: Jagati refers to the base platform on which the temple is constructed.
option_4: Jagati is the sanctum wall that contains inscriptions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jagati refers to the base platform on which the temple is constructed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• In the architectural vocabulary of Nagara-style Hindu temples (the predominant temple architectural style of North India), the "Jagati" refers to the raised base platform upon which the entire temple structure is constructed, serving both a structural/foundational function and often a ceremonial/processional purpose (providing space for circumambulation, "pradakshina," around the temple exterior at an elevated level).

• The Jagati is distinct from other key architectural components of a Nagara temple, such as the "Garbhagriha" (the innermost sanctum housing the main deity), the "Shikhara" (the curvilinear superstructure/spire rising above the sanctum), and the "Mandapa" (the pillared assembly hall preceding the sanctum) — each term referring to a specific, distinct structural element within the temple's overall architectural composition.

• Understanding this precise architectural terminology (Jagati, Garbhagriha, Shikhara, Mandapa, Amalaka, Kalasha, etc.) is a recurring theme in Indian art and culture-focused competitive examination questions, given its importance in describing and classifying India's rich temple architectural heritage.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Nagara-style temples are broadly distinguished from the Dravida (South Indian) and Vesara (hybrid, Deccan) styles primarily through differences in their shikhara (superstructure) design — Nagara temples typically feature a curvilinear shikhara, often topped with a circular "Amalaka" and a crowning pot-shaped "Kalasha" finial, in contrast to the stepped, pyramidal towers (vimana/gopuram) characteristic of Dravidian temple architecture.

• Famous examples of Nagara-style temple architecture include the temples of Khajuraho (Madhya Pradesh), the Sun Temple at Konark (Odisha), and the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple, showcasing the elevated jagati platforms and characteristic curvilinear shikhara design typical of this northern Indian architectural tradition.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Spire housing the deity): This description actually corresponds more closely to the "Garbhagriha" (sanctum sanctorum), which houses the main deity, combined with the Shikhara (the spire/superstructure rising above it) — not the term "Jagati," which specifically refers to the base platform, not a spire.

• Option 2 (Topmost element of shikhara): This description corresponds to elements like the "Amalaka" (the ribbed, disc-shaped stone) or "Kalasha" (the crowning finial) at the very top of the shikhara, not to "Jagati," which refers to the temple's base platform, not its topmost architectural feature.

• Option 4 (Sanctum wall with inscriptions): This does not accurately describe "Jagati" either; temple inscriptions are typically found on various structural walls or dedicated inscription slabs/plaques, not specifically defined by or synonymous with the term "Jagati," which specifically denotes the temple's foundational base platform.

question: What is the principal source of energy for life on Earth?
option_1: Water
option_2: Sunlight
option_3: Soil
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sunlight.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sunlight (solar energy) is the principal, fundamental source of energy sustaining nearly all life on Earth, primarily through the process of photosynthesis, in which green plants, algae, and certain bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy (stored in glucose/organic compounds), forming the foundational base of virtually all terrestrial and aquatic food chains and food webs.

• Nearly all other forms of usable energy on Earth — including fossil fuels (which are essentially stored ancient solar energy captured by long-dead organisms), wind energy (driven by solar-heating-induced atmospheric circulation), and the water cycle (evaporation driven by solar heating) — can ultimately be traced back, directly or indirectly, to the Sun as their primary original energy source.

• This makes sunlight the correct answer to the fundamental biological/ecological question of life's principal energy source, distinguishing it from other important but secondary or derived resources (water, soil, wind) that, while essential to life and ecosystems, do not themselves serve as the primary energy input driving biological energy production.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• A small minority of ecosystems — notably certain deep-sea hydrothermal vent communities — derive their primary energy not from sunlight but from chemosynthesis (using chemical energy from compounds like hydrogen sulfide), representing a rare and specialised exception to the general rule of solar-driven life on Earth.

• The Sun's energy output reaching Earth is harnessed both biologically (through photosynthesis) and, increasingly, technologically (through solar photovoltaic and solar thermal energy systems), reflecting sunlight's dual significance for both natural ecological processes and modern renewable energy strategies.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Water): While water is absolutely essential for all known life processes, it is not itself an energy source; it functions instead as a vital solvent, medium for biochemical reactions, and habitat, rather than providing usable energy input for biological processes.

• Option 3 (Soil): Soil provides essential nutrients and physical support for plant growth, but it is not itself an energy source for life; the energy plants use for growth is derived from sunlight via photosynthesis, not directly from soil.

• Option 4 (Wind): Wind, while a useful renewable energy resource for human technological applications (wind turbines), is not the principal biological energy source for life on Earth; wind itself is, in fact, ultimately driven by solar heating of the atmosphere, making it a secondary, derived phenomenon rather than life's primary energy source.

question: What CRISPR-Cas9 breakthrough was achieved by Indian scientists at IGIB in 2024?

• This work reflects India's growing scientific capability in advanced genomic medicine and gene-editing technology, aligning with the government's broader National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission, aimed at addressing this significant public health challenge, particularly among tribal communities where the disease has historically had a high prevalence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

• CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing technology, for which its pioneers Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, has opened transformative possibilities for treating a range of genetic diseases by directly correcting disease-causing mutations at the DNA level.

 

NOTE

question: The 'Dahi Handi' human pyramid event is central to which festival?

• This tradition symbolically re-enacts childhood stories of Lord Krishna's playful mischief, particularly his fondness for stealing butter and curd (as "Makhan Chor," the butter thief) from homes in his native Vrindavan/Gokul, a beloved and central motif within Krishna devotional folklore.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Janmashtami is celebrated across India (and among Hindu communities worldwide) with various regional customs, including fasting, midnight prayers/aarti marking Krishna's traditional birth hour, temple decorations, and devotional singing (bhajans/kirtans), alongside the distinctive Dahi Handi tradition especially prominent in Maharashtra.

• The human-pyramid Dahi Handi formations have, in recent years, drawn attention (and periodic regulatory/safety guidelines, including height restrictions) due to safety concerns associated with the sometimes very tall, multi-tier pyramid structures formed during these competitive celebrations.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Navratri): A major Hindu festival honouring the goddess Durga/Devi across nine nights, celebrated with practices like Garba/Dandiya dance and fasting, entirely unrelated to the Dahi Handi tradition, which is specifically linked to Krishna Janmashtami.

• Option 2 (Holi): The "Festival of Colours," celebrating the arrival of spring and the triumph of good over evil (via the Holika-Prahlada narrative), involving colour-throwing rather than the Dahi Handi human-pyramid tradition.

question: The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution deals with:
option_1: Panchayats
option_2: Division of powers (lists)
option_3: Fundamental Duties
solution_text:
The correct answer is Division of powers (lists).

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, read alongside Article 246, contains the three legislative lists — the Union List (List I), the State List (List II), and the Concurrent List (List III) — which together define the distribution of legislative powers between the Union (Central) government and the State governments across India's federal structure.

• The Union List comprises subjects of national importance where only Parliament can legislate (e.g., defence, foreign affairs, currency); the State List comprises subjects where only State Legislatures can legislate (e.g., police, public health, agriculture); and the Concurrent List comprises subjects where both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate (e.g., education, forests, criminal law), with Union law generally prevailing in case of conflict (Article 254).

• This division of legislative powers, as detailed in the Seventh Schedule, forms one of the most fundamental structural features of India's federal constitutional design, precisely delineating the respective law-making domains of the Union and State governments.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Subjects can be moved between lists through constitutional amendment — for instance, Education was shifted from the State List to the Concurrent List via the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — reflecting the Seventh Schedule's capacity for periodic reform in response to evolving governance needs.

• Article 248, dealing with "residuary powers" (matters not covered by any of the three lists), vests such residual legislative authority exclusively in Parliament, complementing the specific, enumerated subject-matter distribution laid out in the Seventh Schedule itself.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (Panchayats): Provisions relating to Panchayats (rural local self-government) are primarily covered under Part IX of the Constitution (added by the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992), not the Seventh Schedule, which deals with legislative-power distribution between Union and States, not local self-government structure.

• Option 3 (Fundamental Duties): Fundamental Duties are enumerated under Article 51A, in Part IVA of the Constitution (added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976), an entirely separate constitutional provision from the Seventh Schedule's legislative-list framework.

• Option 4 (Emergency provisions): Emergency provisions are covered under Part XVIII of the Constitution (Articles 352-360), dealing with National, State, and Financial Emergencies — a distinct constitutional subject matter from the Seventh Schedule's legislative-powers-distribution framework.

question: The office of the Speaker in the Indian Parliamentary system is heavily influenced by:
option_1: British Constitution
option_2: Canadian Constitution
option_3: French Constitution
solution_text:
The correct answer is British Constitution.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The office of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha (and, correspondingly, State Legislative Assembly Speakers) in India's parliamentary system is modelled substantially on the British Westminster system, particularly the office of the Speaker of the British House of Commons, reflecting India's broader adoption of the parliamentary form of government from the British constitutional tradition.

• Like the British Speaker, the Indian Speaker's role embodies principles of presiding impartially over legislative proceedings, maintaining order and decorum in the House, and conventionally relinquishing overt party political activity/affiliation once in office (in the British tradition especially, of the Speaker distancing from active partisan politics), reflecting the deep institutional influence of the British parliamentary model on India's own Speaker's office.

• This reflects India's broader constitutional heritage: while India's Constitution draws selectively from multiple international constitutional sources (e.g., the fundamental rights framework draws influence from the US Constitution, and Directive Principles from the Irish Constitution), the parliamentary system of government itself — including the Speaker's office and its conventions — is predominantly drawn from the British constitutional model.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's Constitution is often described as a "borrowed constitution" in a positive, deliberate sense, incorporating well-considered features from multiple global constitutional traditions — including federalism from Canada, the Directive Principles from Ireland, Fundamental Rights largely from the US, and the overall parliamentary system (including the Speaker's office) from Britain.

• The Speaker of the Lok Sabha holds a constitutionally significant role, including presiding over House proceedings, certifying Money Bills, and exercising a casting vote in case of a tie, alongside authority over disqualification proceedings under the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule).

 

NOTE

 

• Option 2 (Canadian Constitution): India's Constitution draws from the Canadian Constitution primarily in relation to features like a strong Centre-oriented federal structure and the concept of residuary powers vested in the Centre, not specifically the Speaker's office, which is more directly modelled on the British system.

• Option 3 (French Constitution): India's Constitution draws from the French Constitution primarily for concepts like "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity" reflected in the Preamble, not for the specific institutional design of the Speaker's office.

• Option 4 (Irish Constitution): India's Constitution draws from the Irish Constitution primarily for the Directive Principles of State Policy and the method of electing the President, not for the specific institutional model of the Speaker's office, which is derived from the British parliamentary tradition instead.

question: The Attorney-General of India has the right of audience in:
option_1: The Supreme Court
option_2: The High Courts
option_3: All courts in India
solution_text:
The correct answer is All courts in India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under Article 76(2) of the Indian Constitution, the Attorney-General of India — the Union government's highest law officer, appointed by the President — has the "right of audience in all courts in India," meaning they are constitutionally entitled to appear, plead, and be heard in any court within the country, not restricted merely to the Supreme Court or High Courts alone.

• This broad right of audience reflects the Attorney-General's comprehensive constitutional role as the chief legal advisor to the Government of India, tasked with representing the Union government's legal interests and providing legal advice across the full spectrum of India's judicial system, whenever required.

• In practice, the Attorney-General typically focuses primarily on significant matters before the Supreme Court and, at times, the High Courts, given the nature of the cases requiring the highest levels of government legal representation, but their constitutional right of audience formally extends to all courts in India, not being limited by any specific court-level restriction.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Attorney-General also has the right to participate in the proceedings of Parliament (though without voting rights), reflecting their unique constitutional position bridging the executive and legislative branches' legal-advisory needs.

• The Attorney-General is assisted in their duties by the Solicitor General of India and several Additional Solicitors General, who handle various aspects of government legal representation across different courts and cases, working within the broader framework of India's law-officer system.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 (The Supreme Court): Incorrect as a standalone/limiting answer — while the Attorney-General does frequently appear before the Supreme Court, their constitutional right of audience is not limited to the Supreme Court alone; it extends to all courts in India.

• Option 2 (The High Courts): Incorrect as a standalone/limiting answer — similarly, while the Attorney-General may appear before High Courts, their right of audience is not restricted specifically to High Courts; it constitutionally covers all courts in the country.

• Option 4 (Constitutional courts): Incorrect — India does not have a formally separate category of "constitutional courts" distinct from its regular court hierarchy (Supreme Court, High Courts, subordinate courts all handle constitutional matters as part of their jurisdiction); the Attorney-General's right of audience specifically and explicitly extends to all courts in India under Article 76(2), not a specially defined "constitutional courts" category.
